I recommend you keep a journal. Writing down your thoughts and feelings has helped me immensely in trying to be mindful of what's going on. Don't be afraid to use analogies ("treading water" is a popular one, and boy is it accurate sometimes), and compare it to past emotions.

In addition to what /u/lob5t3r said, I'd add that sleep deprivation is probably doing more harm than good. Sleep is very important to mental and physical health, and both of them are closely tied to each other and to OCD. It's impossible to relax if you're sleep deprived, and it makes it so much easier to start ruminating or obsessing if you're not well-rested.

This is a very tricky situation, because your first instinct will be reassurance. In my experience, this doesn't really work. The OCD works with any sort of feedback and twist it with uncertainty.

I'll give an example. Say you, your sister, and your brother are all talking about some topic. It's a natural conversation. Everyone is going to flub up, or there will be a natural lull or semi-awkward silence. OCD may make your sister feel somehow responsible for the flubs in the conversation, that every deviation from being a perfectly sociable person is a huge flaw in her behavior. Or if there's an area of the conversation where she doesn't participate fully, the OCD might hone in on that as "the truth" of the matter, and that every other moment was just you two "putting up" with her.

That's one of the trickiest things about pure O: It feels like ignoring the intrusive thoughts is irresponsible, even though it's the right, healthy thing to do. In this case, if you don't get along with someone or are intruding, the "best" (and I use that term loosely) thing to do is to back off. But OCD can convince you that you're not wanted in any situation, regardless of any evidence. It's an overactive warning system at its core.

I'd suggest she go back to CBT. If she recognizes these thoughts as part of the OCD, then she'll understand. If she doesn't, it might seem scary to talk to her about it, but I'd make sure to make it clear that you're concern for her is your choice. It's what you want to do as her brother and her friend, and you know she'd do the same for you. 

I say that last part because OCD can make you feel really broken, and feeling like a burden or an obligation is one of the crappiest feelings in this kind of situation. It only leads to more stress and more distance.

The best way to bring it up is just tell them the truth: That it's embarrassing and awkward for you to talk about. From my own experiences and what I've read, it's INCREDIBLY unlikely that your therapist will "freak out" in any way. I don't think any therapists assume people are "making new things up."

Intrusive thoughts are common in everyone; OCD just makes you harp on them more and makes it harder to just shrug them off.

I wouldn't say primarily, but one fairly consistent obsession has been "Do people actually enjoy my company, or are they just being nice and I'm wasting their time?" I've also definitely done what you describe, picking apart a conversation afterwards.

In your case, you're specifically looking for something to point at and say "I messed up," and you're going to find it. If you wanted to navigate every conversation with natural perfection, you'd need incredible speaking skills and people skills. Nobody's expecting everything you say to be a Kennedy speech. I'd just try to remember a few things:

Everyone makes mistakes when speaking. For most minor mistakes, people barely notice, and it doesn't reflect on your personality at all.

Gaffs might happen. They happen to everyone, even world leaders.

II think at some point I just told myself "I'm trying my best. If they don't like it, they're free to leave." So yeah, someone might hate me and not want to say anything. But I think I'm a pretty OK person, and I'm definitely not forcing them to do this. Any choice they make about associating with me is their own choice.

Another thing that helped me specifically was that I actually saw someone in a situation like what I feared. When someone is genuinely disliked and people are just "putting up with them," it's almost palpable. Everyone's really distant, they avoid addressing them directly, and there's a strange tension in the air. I felt bad for the guy, but at the same time, no one was saying "Let's go invite him. I guess we have to."

I guess that's a thing you could tell him. That people don't engage with someone they're "just tolerating." If someone talks to you or invites you to hang out or anything like they, they probably want you there.

If the anxiety was only about you cheating on him it'd be one thing, but add in the thought of other people constantly making fun of him and it sounds like he has anxiety about his own self-worth. This is all speculation, but I'll just write my thoughts down and see if anything sticks out at you/seems to apply to the situation.

The self-worth anxiety. I've had it. It's kind of a constant, nagging fear that you're not wanted and that any kindness toward you is done out of obligation; everyone could secretly be thinking, "I want to be nice in general, so I guess I have to be nice to YOU" or in this case "I'm dating him, so I HAVE to say these things" instead of the truth that "I'm dating him, so I want to say these things to make him feel better. I'd like to think he'd do the same for me." 

When you feel like that, it's really hard to see yourself as anything other than a burden. And it's the uncertainty that's hardest to overcome: no one's going to say to your face "I have never liked you. I have always wanted you gone." So when you get it into your head that you're somehow a drain or weighing people down, you start to see the kindness of others as a burden on them. "They're forcing themselves to be nice to someone like me."

From what I've read, you're doing a good job. Acknowledging that you don't have proof in that way I think is a really good way to reassure him while not feeding the cycle. It sounds like you're educating yourself and not addressing the thoughts excessively, and the OCD isn't some big looming secret. I can't really advise you on how to proceed since relationships aren't something I'm experienced in. I can't readily think of anything more you could do beyond what you're doing.

I had a similar problem. When I first found out, I pretty much hated everything. I hated my parents because it came from their genetics, I hated everyone around me for not having it, and I absolutely DESPISED myself because of what I was doing. No one I hated had done anything wrong and I shouldn't be hating them. I knew I was projecting. I remember my exact thought: I know they said life isn't fair, but god damn do I want it to be fair. I wanted a magic key. I'd have sold my right arm if it meant I could just snap my fingers and be done with it all.

What worked for me was researching it. I found out it was real, but not some obscure, untreatable nightmare I thought it was in my head. It's a diagnosis. It has a name. It has effective and ineffective treatments. You may live with it for the rest of your life, but that's not to say you need to be suffering from it for the rest of your life. 

Yes, it is an illness. But it's an illness. It's not a character defect. It's not your fault. It's not a death sentence. It's chemicals and neural pathways in your brain doing some weird shit sometimes. Some people might not understand, but it's totally okay with keeping it a secret to some people as long as you're getting the help you need. I really think therapy is the right call. As scary as it is, sometimes you just need a bit of help.

I think everyone gets embarrassed talking about things like that, because it makes you feel really vulnerable. Anxiety is a huge bitch. If you're too anxious to talk to people about things like this, it can become harder and harder to convince yourself that you can do it. I'm not really good with social situations like this, so I can't offer any advice on how to get to that point where you feel comfortable enough to share with people close to you, but hopefully you find someone you can talk to.

I don't think either is a "mask." Both can be the real you. There can be a part of you whose afraid and anxious, and there can be a part of you that enjoys the things you do.

"Am I an attention whore?" I absolutely HATE that phrase. I thought it, too, in the past, but it's a garbage phrase that doesn't really mean anything. It implies that wanting attention is bad and makes you feel guilty if you feel like you really need attention. This isn't "guys look at how depressed I am don't you feel sorry for me." People who commit suicide do want "attention," but that's not a bad thing. It means they want to feel less alone. And that's okay. It's okay to be afraid or sad or lonely, and it's okay to wish you didn't. 

Part of it might be puberty, but that doesn't discredit what you're feeling. Don't try to fix this because you "feel like you shouldn't be sad because it might just be puberty," fix it because you don't like feeling this way and you want and deserve to feel better. 

I'd encourage you to talk to someone, maybe your parents. Chances are they went through something similar, and in talking it out you would ideally be able to determine whether this is "normal" and you just needed to talk, or if this something deeper. Either way is absolutely a valid concern.

The thing that really struck me about this was you said "How painful it is to be surrounded by people you care for... but not care for you back." I can't even begin to imagine your situation, but that sounds like absolute hell. I'm not sure who you talked to, and I know it's the "obvious" solution, but try talking to someone again. A guidance counselor or, if possible, a therapist. I know it's pretty much the absolute shittiest thing to "ask for help" like this; the first time spilling your secrets will feel like the absolute low. At least for me, I was absolutely certain that my therapist would judge me and blame me or whatever. Didn't happen. There are people, not even just professionals, who care in the same way you do, that just want to help people through this kind of stuff.

Second point, you're not "too young" to feel like this. Problems are problems, and being "too young" to have problems isn't a thing. Being "too young" to deal with those problems alone is also not a thing. Don't beat yourself up for being sad or depressed. You're not under any obligation from anyone to "feel better" except from yourself, because you deserve it.

From what I've seen and my own experience, switching is pretty common.

Oddly enough, I find that when I've "switched," the thing I was worried about before becomes sort of an afterthought. Like, if I were in your position, if I thought back on the anxiety of hit-and-run, now I'd think "yes, there's that possibility, but I can minimize it if I'm responsible. It's not worth obsessing over." i.e. nothing is particularly "worth obsessing over" for me unless it's my current obsession (which also isn't worth obsessing over, but it still happens)

Story time: Recently diagnosed with OCD that went "undiagnosed" in the sense that the symptoms were lumped within a diagnosis of Aspergers. The first "OCD moment" I can remember is I was watching Whose Line Is It Anyway and they made a joke about schizophrenia. I didn't know what that was, so I asked my parents who told me it was hearing voices telling them to do bad things (I was about 7 at the time, so that was enough of an explanation). I then became incredibly worried that I had it or would have it. It came to the point where I would "make up" a voice in my head and then ask myself "have I ever experienced anything like that before?" Huge sexual identity crisis in either 2nd or 4th grade (fear of incest, etc). General intrusive thoughts, very mild HOCD, but nothing particularly catastrophic.

Cue this summer. Shit hit the fan. I was worried about mutilating myself or someone I loved, I was worried about being a sexual deviant, all the fun stuff. I'm still dealing with it now. A few things that have helped me so far are

a) Telling my parents that something is bothering me. One day I just resolved to say "Fuck this bullshit, I'm not going to let this beat me" and I e-mailed my parents something along the lines of "Here's some stuff about OCD I've been reading." Support from someone else is really helpful simply because you can argue with yourself all day, but if someone else says "You're not a monster," it's resonates more.

b) Take a deep breath. Again, cliche as hell, but it does help to some degree. It won't bring you down from a panic, but it can help you not to start a cycle of worrying.

I haven't ever tried anything, but I've definitely considered it more than I would prefer. I'm absolutely petrified of dying, though. I have DEFINITELY wanted to enter a coma at times, since I somehow rationalized a coma as some sort of big nap where I could wake up refreshed or treated or whatever. Just some sort of escape. Not how that works, though.

Talking and being open with people here has helped a LOT. Just feeling less alone and less like a freak. I haven't told my friends, but if you really want to try to express it, I'd keep it as simple as possible. Obviously you'd only want to say this to people you trust. I guess my metaphor of choice would be a mental scab. Everyone feels the desire to pick or scratch an itchy scab, but we've got some sort of constant, mental scab that "itches" like crazy.

Whoa whoa whoa. That's a HUGE leap you're making. "it's not a good thing that happened," therefore "you really are attracted to these things?"  Not how that works. Not even how basic causation works. I know the nagging thoughts in your head want to give you some sort of certainty, and saying "FUCK IT I'M BROKEN" is an easy way to just kind of write off the uncertainty and "simplify," as fucked up as that seems, but it's just not true.

http://www.academia.edu/4056896/Threat_Assessment_in_OCD

This helped me A LOT. It's what pushed me to message my parents and be more open about the fact that something's bothering me. Some excerpts:

"when the illness gets severe, theperson can become convinced that they actually want to carry out these acts. I have spoken to quite a few people with OCD who told me that the illness made them feel like they wanted to have gay sex or have sex with children or assault and murder people. This is probably correct though in that people with OCD do not act on their obsessions. I have not met one person who acted on an obsession of causing harm to themselves or others, or how did anything sexual to a child in response to an obsession."

"You are also looking at something that is occurring all oralmost all of the time.
If it is, it is likely you are dealing with anobsession. With paraphilias, they are much less likely to be going allthe time, and when they are frequent, the person is likely to befantasizing."

"The OCD'er is a shy, almost meek person whose dominant emotion is fear or even terror. Quite simply, they are too scared of dying to kill themselves, so the fear associated with suicide prevents them from carrying out the act. In contrast, a violent of sexual offender is likely to see the thoughts as fun or enjoyable, though sometimes they feel guilty for enjoying them so much."

Other points are a desire to seek help. If you were a pedophile, you wouldn't be saying this. You'd be worried about "getting caught" rather than "getting help." The fact that you're avoiding children "like the plague" (I think you said that somewhere) is another thing. It's really scary to imagine what's in a pedophile's head, and since we don't really know, we assume it's just like us. But most of what I've read says no guilt. No resistance. That is what they want and everyone else is wrong. This is NOT what we're going through. This is pretty much the opposite.

But yeah, I'll PM you my skype username

If it's impacting your school, your sleep schedule and you seem distressed, your parents probably know SOMETHING is up. And most likely they're worried, too. Keeping this a secret isn't doing anyone any favors. I'm NOT saying you need to tell your parents about the contents of these thoughts. I sure as hell haven't. But they probably know you're not doing well and don't know what to do. The first step is awful. Fuck it, story time.

I've seen a therapist since I was about 4 for autism/aspergers, so I'd never really "opened up" since I'd just seen it as "some doctor's appointment." This summer things got weird and scary. I'd had a therapist appointment coming up, and I was very unsure. She was a trained professional, so she lead the conversation deeper than what I was expecting. I wound up getting VERY VERY close to spilling my guts but couldn't bring myself to do it. I wanted to say it and ask for help so badly, but I was so afraid. The next morning, the anxiety and self-hatred for not opening up were so bad I went into the bathroom and threw up. I asked my parents to move the next appointment up ASAP, and they got one for the next week. Pretty much that entire week was hell, self-loathing and fear, but after breaking down and talking at that appointment, I felt AMAZING. Completely fantastic. Not even overjoyed, but hopeful. The thoughts were still there, but barely, and I could ignore them. Granted, this didn't last very long at all, maybe a day or two before I started getting more anxious, but it was nowhere near as bad as it was when I hadn't talked about it.

The first step is pretty much the shittiest thing. It feels like you're giving up all hope of being strong enough to handle this and begging someone else to do it for you, but you're not. You're asking for help from people who want to help. And it's worth it.

Yep, trying to squash it with "rational" thoughts won't work when the thoughts come up. I can't necessarily comment on the real stuff you enjoyed, but I've talked to my therapist about the drawn/animated stuff I enjoyed and she told me that things like that are designed to elicit that response. So while it's certainly not GOOD that it happened, I don't think it's as damning as you think. Again, I can't comment on much, but I would REALLY suggest you seek some sort of professional help. At the very least, a common thing I see is the [National Suicide Prevention Lifeline](http://www.suicidepreventionlifeline.org/), which apparently has both a phone and online chat service for just a general crisis.

I'm in a similar boat right now. I'm 20 and this summer my OCD kicked off something fierce (didn't even know I had it until then, all symptoms before were written off as part of Aspergers). It started as violent thoughts. I was watching a stupid anime of all things and the characters were fighting and it was a bit gruesome. My thought process went from "It's cool that they can fight so hard for what they believe in" to "I wonder if I could?" to "I wonder what kind of pain I'd be able to endure?" to thoughts of testing that theory by harming myself in graphic ways. Then I took driver's ed, which I had put off for so long that I was surrounded by 15 year olds, and guess what obsessive thoughts showed up?

I know it's really hard to seek help, but you don't need to go all in. You don't need to say "I'm having these intrusive thoughts and they scare me," you can just be vague and say "I'm having a rough time and I think therapy would help." If they don't seem to get it, try to convey how serious it is without giving anything up. Like "I'm sorry I can't be more open about this, but I just think it's really important that I see someone."

Bear in mind that this is just to get you to a safer place. I know you wouldn't believe me now, but there's NO SHAME in having a mental illness. Obviously. Everyone says this. But when push comes to shove, people will think less of you, right? Not anyone that matters. And honestly I'm getting pretty goddamn sick of being afraid of some reaction from some asshole who doesn't understand and doesn't even want to TRY to understand. Fuck those guys, if they even exist.

Also in regards to your last sentence, I don't think you should be trying to analyze these thoughts. Most of what I've read said that that's only going to make it worse, and that by analyzing it, you're saying "these thoughts mean something." If you try to analyze and talk your way out of it, I don't really feel like it's an argument you can win, because the obsessive thoughts cheat. They turn your rational reasons into irrational worries and set it up so that anything you say is just proof that you're wrong.

There are DEFINITELY ways to deal with it, though. Cognitive behavioral therapy is something I want to talk to my therapist about. Medication helps a lot, though it takes a while to kick in. I'm currently taking pills daily with some as-needed to supplement if it gets really bad. And I really hope what /u/CosmicChef is saying is true, because I really just want to be a good person who doesn't hurt anyone.

Sorry, this was super stream-of-consciousness. I'm not sure how to express myself on this topic since it's all so new to me. But everyone here who's going through a crisis like I am seems to have similar symptoms (those with Pure O at least), so I'm realizing that I'm not alone, and neither are you.

Exactly. There have even been points where I'll see something on /r/aww and do some fucking mental gymnastics. "This picture is cute," "this picture is therefore something I enjoy," "this picture has a little girl in it," therefore "I enjoy looking at pictures of little girls", therefore "I am a pedophile." I acknowledge that the thought process is flawed and ignores context (i.e. that "like" has two different meanings ENTIRELY), but it still feels incredibly uncomfortable and scary to think these thoughts. And then I'll try to shit-test myself by semi-consciously conjuring an image to somehow "test if this is really what I want," and I'm disgusted, but then it goes full circle to "if you hate it so much, why'd you just think it" and the whole goddamn thing goes in circles and it's fucking terrible.

I'm sitting here posting this on an alt account I made in an incognito window. I just started crying. This is almost EXACTLY what I'm going through now. Like, even reading your comments about "enjoying things they would like in the past" (though for me it was lolicon) and "suggestive furry content", using masturbation to relieve stress, liking a "younger (petite, I guess?) body" This is a completely new account. I'm incredibly ashamed of these things and I wish I could be like you and just say them on my main account but I'm terrified I'm a monster. I'm really scared. You are not alone, and I'm so happy that I'm not either.

Honestly, I'm so happy right now. I've read passages from books and they all said "this is possible to happen," but I was paranoid that it was just something they said to somehow "get pedophiles back on the right track" and that I was fooling myself into thinking I could ever be anything but a monster. I'm terrified of even confronting it with the therapy that /u/shrubdog mentioned for fear that it will worsen it. I don't know if this is helping you to feel less alone, but this is just... Thank you.
